claim: Approximately 2 billion people have been infected with human hepatitis B virus (HBV) worldwide.
source_text: Approximately 2 billion people have been infected with human hepatitis B virus (HBV) worldwide.
evidence_reasoning: This is a widely cited epidemiological statistic that draws from established public health knowledge about HBV prevalence.

claim: Over 350 million people currently are chronically infected with HBV and are at high risk for progression to cirrhosis, liver failure, or cancer.
source_text: Over 350 million people currently are chronically infected and are at high risk for progression to cirrhosis, liver failure, or cancer.
evidence_reasoning: This represents established epidemiological data about chronic HBV infection prevalence and associated risks.

claim: More than 50% of liver cancers worldwide are attributed to HBV infection.
source_text: More than 50% of liver cancers worldwide are attributed to HBV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is a well-established epidemiological fact about the relationship between HBV and liver cancer.

claim: HBV-related liver diseases cause approximately 1 million deaths per year.
source_text: HBV-related liver diseases remain a major public health problem, causing approximately 1 million deaths per year.
evidence_reasoning: This is a widely cited mortality statistic from public health literature.

claim: Individuals coinfected with HBV and HDV are at greater risk for rapid progression and severe disease.
source_text: Individuals coinfected with HBV and HDV are at greater risk for rapid progression and severe disease
evidence_reasoning: This represents established clinical knowledge about HBV-HDV coinfection outcomes.

claim: The pre-S1 domain of the large envelope protein is a key determinant for receptor(s) binding.
source_text: The pre-S1 domain of the large envelope protein is a key determinant for receptor(s) binding.
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge in the field, supported by previous research on HBV envelope proteins.

claim: The receptor-binding region of pre-S1 specifically interacts with sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP).
source_text: by using near zero distance photo-cross-linking and tandem affinity purification, we revealed that the receptor-binding region of pre-S1 specifically interacts with sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP)
evidence_reasoning: This claim is supported by experimental data from photo-cross-linking and tandem affinity purification experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane transporter predominantly expressed in the liver.
source_text: sodium taurocholate cotransporting polypeptide (NTCP), a multiple transmembrane transporter predominantly expressed in the liver
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about NTCP's structure and tissue distribution.

claim: Silencing NTCP inhibited HBV and HDV infection.
source_text: Silencing NTCP inhibited HBV and HDV infection
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data from siRNA knockdown experiments shown in Figure 4.

claim: Exogenous NTCP expression rendered nonsusceptible hepatocarcinoma cells susceptible to HBV and HDV infections.
source_text: exogenous NTCP expression rendered nonsusceptible hepatocarcinoma cells susceptible to these viral infections
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing viral infection in NTCP-transfected cells (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: Replacing amino acids 157–165 of nonfunctional monkey NTCP with the human counterpart conferred its ability in supporting both viral infections.
source_text: Moreover, replacing amino acids 157–165 of nonfunctional monkey NTCP with the human counterpart conferred its ability in supporting both viral infections.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data from mutagenesis studies shown in Figure 7.

claim: NTCP is a functional receptor for HBV and HDV.
source_text: Our results demonstrate that NTCP is a functional receptor for HBV and HDV.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is based on multiple lines of experimental evidence including binding, knockdown, and complementation studies.

claim: An N-terminal myristoylated peptide corresponding to amino acids 2–48 of the pre-S1 domain effectively blocks both HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes.
source_text: An N-terminal myristoylated peptide corresponding to amino acids (aa) 2–48 of the pre-S1 domain of the L protein has been shown to effectively block both HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by citations to previous work (Barrera et al., 2005; Glebe et al., 2005; Gripon et al., 2005; Engelke et al., 2006; Schulze et al., 2010).

claim: L-photo-leucine contains a photoactivatable diazirine ring that yields a reactive carbene group upon UV irradiation at 365 nm.
source_text: L-photo-leucine contains a photoactivatable diazirine ring. Irradiation of ultraviolet (UV) light at 365 nm induces a loss of nitrogen of the diazirine ring and yields a reactive carbene group with short half-life for covalent cross-linking at nearly zero distance
evidence_reasoning: This describes the known chemical properties of L-photo-leucine, supported by citation to Suchanek et al., 2005.

claim: Primary hepatocytes isolated from treeshrews (Tupaia belangeri) are susceptible to human HBV infection.
source_text: Primary hepatocytes isolated from treeshrews (Tupaia belangeri), the only species susceptible to human HBV infection other than humans and chimpanzees
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge supported by citations (Su et al., 1987; Walter et al., 1996; Glebe et al., 2003).

claim: Leu11 is 100% conserved among HBV genotypes.
source_text: Leu11 is 100% conserved among HBV genotypes
evidence_reasoning: This is based on sequence analysis of HBV genotypes, representing established knowledge in the field.

claim: Changing phe14 to leucine (F14L) did not significantly affect the binding of HDV virion to primary Tupaia hepatocytes.
source_text: Changing phe14 to leucine (F14L) did not significantly affect the binding of HDV virion to primary Tupaia hepatocytes (PTHs) (Figure 1B).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: WTb inhibited HDV binding to PTHs with efficiency comparable to Myr-47/WT.
source_text: WTb inhibited HDV binding to PTHs with efficiency comparable to Myr-47/WT that is comprised of all natural amino acids (Figure 1A,C).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: N9Kb peptide did not block HDV binding to PTHs.
source_text: A peptide Myr-47/N9Kb (or N9Kb hereafter) similar to WTb but with an additional mutation at the ninth residue (N9K) did not block HDV binding to PTHs (Figure 1C).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: WTb but not N9Kb inhibited viral infection of HBV and HDV on PTHs.
source_text: WTb but not N9Kb inhibited viral infection of HBV and HDV on PTHs (Figure 1D).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The protein cross-linked by WTb is sensitive to PNGase F treatment and shifted from ∼65 to ∼43 kDa.
source_text: The protein cross-linked by WTb is sensitive to PNGase F treatment and shifted from ∼65 to ∼43 kDa.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A, indicating the protein is glycosylated.

claim: Non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT peptide but not its N9K mutant competed with WTb peptide for cross-linking with PTHs in a dose-dependent manner.
source_text: Non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT peptide (WT) but not its N9K mutant competed with 200 nM of WTb peptide for cross-linking with PTHs in a dose-dependent manner.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B, demonstrating specificity of binding.

claim: The abundance of the target protein(s) in PTH cells decreased over time in culture.
source_text: The abundance of the target protein(s) in PTH cells decreased over time.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C showing decreased cross-linking over days in culture.

claim: WTb cross-linked with a glycoprotein of molecular weight at ∼60 kDa in primary human hepatocytes, which shifted to ∼39 kDa upon PNGase F treatment.
source_text: 200 nM WTb but not N9Kb cross-linked with a glycoprotein of molecular weight at ∼60 kDa, which shifted to ∼39 kDa upon PNGase F treatment.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D for primary human hepatocytes.

claim: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) was identified as the common protein hit in MS analysis of the ∼65- and ∼43-kDa bands from WTb cross-linked samples.
source_text: The common protein hit identified by MS analysis of the ∼65- and ∼43-kDa bands cut from the WTb cross-linked sample was Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 2E and Figure 2—figure supplement 5.

claim: Tupaia NTCP shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart.
source_text: Tupaia NTCP (tsNTCP) shares 83.9% protein sequence identity with its human counterpart
evidence_reasoning: This is based on sequence alignment analysis of the cloned tsNTCP.

claim: Tupaia NTCP has an insertion of 30 aa near its C-terminus compared to human NTCP.
source_text: has an insertion of 30 aa near its C-terminus
evidence_reasoning: This is based on sequence analysis shown in Figure 2F.

claim: WTb but not N9Kb specifically cross-linked with both human and Tupaia NTCP expressed in 293T cells.
source_text: 293T cells transfected with an expression vector or plasmid containing cDNA of hNTCP or tsNTCP fused with a C9 tag at its C-terminus were cross-linked with 200 nM Myr-47/WTb or Myr-N9Kb
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3A demonstrating specific interaction.

claim: WTb peptide colocalized with tsNTCP-EGFP on cell surface.
source_text: 293T cells transfected with tsNTCP-EGFP or a control hSDC2-EGFP (encoding human heparan sulfate proteoglycan core protein fused with EGFP at C-terminus) expression plasmid were incubated with WTb or N9Kb in the presence or absence of 200 nM non-photoreactive Myr-47/WT as indicated. Bound peptides were probed with PE-streptavidin and the colocalization of peptide and NTCP on cell surface was shown in the merged images.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: FITC-pre-S1 peptide binding to Huh-7 cells was enhanced by hNTCP transfection.
source_text: 24 hr post-transfection with hNTCP or a control plasmid, the cells were stained with 200 nM FITC-pre-S1 (FITC-labeled lipopeptide corresponding to the N-terminal 59-amino acid of pre-S1). The binding was analyzed by flow cytometry.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by FACS data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Wild-type HDV but not HDV with N9K mutation showed enhanced binding to Huh-7 cells transfected with hNTCP.
source_text: Huh-7 cells, after 24 hr of transfection of indicated plasmids, were incubated with wild-type HDV or HDV with a N9K mutation on its L protein. Bound virions were quantified by qRT-PCR. The result is presented as fold changes of binding over the background virus binding to pcDNA6-transfected cells.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Knockdown of tsNTCP in PTHs inhibited HDV infection as indicated by reduced HDV genomic and antigenomic RNA levels.
source_text: Freshly isolated PTHs were transfected with siRNAs against tsNTCP or a control siRNA. 3 days later, 1 × 105 PTHs were inoculated with HDV, HBV, or control viruses AAV8-HBV and Lenti-VSV-G. For HDV and HBV, PTHs were infected at 500 and 100 genome equivalent copies per cell, respectively. The level of HDV viral RNAs in infected cells was quantified by qRT-PCR on 6 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating reduced viral RNA upon NTCP knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of tsNTCP in PTHs inhibited HBV infection as indicated by reduced HBsAg and HBeAg secretion.
source_text: For HBV infection, the kinetics of secreted viral antigens HBsAg and HBeAg were measured by ELISA. The medium was changed every 3 days.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4A demonstrating reduced viral antigens upon NTCP knockdown.

claim: Knockdown of tsNTCP did not affect AAV8-HBV infection in PTHs.
source_text: NTCP knockdown did not affect AAV8-HBV infection in PTHs, as shown by the kinetics of HBeAg (Figure 4A, lower-right).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data showing no effect on AAV8-mediated HBV genome delivery, indicating NTCP functions at viral entry.

claim: NTCP has no effect on post-entry steps of HBV infection.
source_text: This result shows that NTCP has no effect on post-entry steps of HBV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the AAV8-HBV control experiment showing NTCP knockdown does not affect viral replication when entry is bypassed.

claim: NTCP mRNA level was low in HepaRG cells before induction but increased dramatically when the cells differentiated after induction.
source_text: The NTCP mRNA level was low in HepaRG cells before induction when examined on days 5 and 10 after initial plating, but increased dramatically when the cells differentiated after induction (Figure 4B, upper-left).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: About 70% HDV infection was reduced by hNTCP knockdown in differentiated HepaRG cells.
source_text: About 70% HDV infection was reduced by hNTCP knockdown as indicated by decreased levels of HDV viral RNAs (Figure 4B, upper-right).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: HBV infection of differentiated HepaRG cells was inhibited by hNTCP knockdown as indicated by reduced HBeAg and viral RNAs.
source_text: Similarly, HBV infection was also inhibited as indicated by significantly reduced HBeAg at multiple time points (Figure 4B, lower-left), as well as viral RNAs including the 3.5 kb RNA for HBV pre-C and pregenome RNA (pgRNA) and HBV total RNA (Figure 4B, lower-right) quantified at the end of the experiment.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Knockdown of hNTCP significantly reduced HBV infection in primary human hepatocytes.
source_text: Consistently, knockdown of hNTCP significantly reduced HBV infection, which was correlated with the NTCP mRNA knockdown efficiency. Both viral antigens and viral RNAs were decreased in cells transfected with hNTCP-specific siRNAs but not with the control siRNA (Figure 4C).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: NTCP is a common key cellular receptor component necessary for HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes.
source_text: Taken together, these data demonstrate NTCP as a common key cellular receptor component necessary for HBV and HDV infections of hepatocytes.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is based on the combined knockdown experiments in multiple cell types showing requirement for NTCP.

claim: NTCP mRNA expression levels in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells were about 10,000 times lower than that in primary human and Tupaia hepatocytes.
source_text: The levels of NTCP mRNA in Huh-7 and HepG2 cells were about 10,000 times lower than that in primary human and Tupaia hepatocytes (Figure 5A).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Transient transfection of hNTCP rendered Huh-7 cells susceptible to HDV infection.
source_text: 1 × 105 Huh-7 cells were transfected with 100 ng hNTCP/pcDNA6 or a vector control in 24-well plate and maintained in PMM, 24 hr after transfection, transfected cells were infected with HDV at 500 genome equivalent copies per cell. On 8 dpi, HDV delta antigen, which typically locates in nuclei, was stained with 4G5 antibody in green
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 5B demonstrating HDV infection in NTCP-transfected cells.

claim: HDV infection of hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells was inhibited by HBV entry inhibitors including HBIG, Myr-59, and anti-HBsAg mAb 17B9.
source_text: Huh-7 cells transfected with hNTCP were infected with HDV similarly as in panel B in the presence or absence of HBV entry inhibitors: HBIG (hepatitis B immune globulin), Myr-59, and anti-HBsAg mAb, 17B9.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5C demonstrating inhibition by known entry blockers.

claim: HDV viral RNAs accumulated over time in hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells after infection.
source_text: Huh-7 cells transfected with hNTCP were infected with HDV similarly as in panel B. The HDV viral RNAs in infected cells at indicated time points were quantified by real-time RT-PCR.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 5D demonstrating viral replication.

claim: HDV infection of hNTCP-transfected Huh-7 cells increased with increasing multiplicities of genome equivalents.
source_text: With 100 ng hNTCP/pcDNA6, 1 × 105 Huh-7 cells were transfected, as in panel B. Transfected cells were infected with increasing mge of HDV as indicated. HDV delta antigen was detected as in panel B on 8 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: HDV infection of Huh-7 cells increased with increasing levels of hNTCP transfection.
source_text: About 1 × 105 Huh-7 cells were transfected with a vector pcDNA6 or hNTCP/pcDNA6 at indicated amounts and cells were inoculated with 500 mge of HDV. HDV delta antigen was detected on 8 dpi as in panel B.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 5F.

claim: Transient transfection of hNTCP rendered HepG2 cells susceptible to HDV infection.
source_text: About 2 × 105 HepG2 cells were transiently transfected with 0.3 µg hNTCP/pcDNA6 or a vector control and maintained in PMM. Cells were infected at 500 mge with HDV 24 hr after transfection. On 8 dpi, HDV delta antigen in infected cells was stained with mAb 4G5 (left) and the HDV viral RNAs were determined by real time RT-PCR.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: HepG2 stable cell line stably expressing hNTCP (HepG2-hNTCP) was established.
source_text: HepG2 stable cell line stably expressing hNTCP (HepG2-hNTCP) was established by G418 selection after transient transfection.
evidence_reasoning: This describes the generation of a stable cell line, confirmed by FITC-pre-S1 staining in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: HDV infection of HepG2-hNTCP stable cells was inhibited by entry inhibitor Myr-59.
source_text: Infection of HDV on HepG2-hNTCP stable cells was conducted in the presence or absence of entry inhibitor 200 nM Myr-59.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 3.

claim: Transient transfection of tsNTCP or hNTCP rendered HepG2 cells susceptible to HBV infection.
source_text: HepG2 cells transiently transfected with either tsNTCP- or hNTCP-supported HBV infection as evidenced by continuous secretion of HBeAg over time and accumulation of HBV replicative intermediate viral RNAs in the infected cells.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HBV infection of NTCP-transfected HepG2 cells was blocked by entry inhibitor Myr-59.
source_text: The entry inhibitor Myr-59 blocked the infection
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: HepG2-hNTCP cells showed intracellular HBsAg expression after HBV infection.
source_text: HepG2-hNTCP stable cells or parental HepG2 cells were inoculated with HBV at 100 mge. On 9 dpi, intracellular HBsAg of infected cells on coverslips was stained with antibody 17B9 in green
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by immunofluorescence data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: HBV-infected HepG2-hNTCP cells secreted HBeAg over time, which was inhibited by entry inhibitors.
source_text: The cells were infected with HBV at 100 mge in the presence or absence of entry inhibitors as indicated. The medium was changed every 2 days. Secreted HBeAg was measured at 3, 5, 7 dpi
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: HBV infection efficiency of HepG2-hNTCP cells is correlated with the viral inoculum dose.
source_text: With increasing dose of HBV, 2 × 105 HepG2-hNTCP cells were infected as indicated. HBV RNAs in infected cells was examined on 10 dpi with real-time RT-PCR for the total HBV RNAs and the 3.5 kb transcripts.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: HBV cccDNA was detected in HepG2-hNTCP cells after infection but not in parental HepG2 cells or in the presence of entry inhibitor Myr-59.
source_text: HepaG2-hNTCP cells or HepG2 parental cells were infected with 100 mge of HBV in the presence or absence of Myr-59. HBV cccDNA was extracted from ∼ 2–3 × 106 infected cells on 7 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by Southern blot data shown in Figure 6D demonstrating authentic HBV infection.

claim: HBV cccDNA levels increased over time in HBV-infected HepG2-hNTCP cells.
source_text: HBV cccDNA (in panel E) was quantified at indicated time points post infection
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by kinetic qPCR data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: HBV RNA levels increased over time in HBV-infected HepG2-hNTCP cells but not in parental HepG2 cells.
source_text: HBV RNA copies (in panel F) in the infected cells were measured at indicated time points, data of similarly infected parental HepG2 cells on 9 dpi were also shown.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by kinetic qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6F.

claim: About 10% HepG2-NTCP cells were infected at multiplicities of genome equivalents of 100, which is comparable to the efficiency of HBV infection of PHHs.
source_text: As shown by intracellular staining of HBV core antigen (HBcAg) on day 8 post-infection, about 10% HepG2-NTCP cells were infected at multiplicities of genome equivalents (mge) of 100, which is comparable to the efficiency of HBV infection of PHHs (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by immunofluorescence quantification shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: The level of secreted HBeAg from HepG2-NTCP appeared to be higher than that in PHHs from two donors.
source_text: The level of secreted HBeAg from HepG2-NTCP appeared to be higher than that in PHHs from two donors
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by comparative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: The levels of viral RNAs per nanogram of total cell RNA in HepG2-NTCP and PHHs are comparable.
source_text: whereas the levels of viral RNAs per nanogram of total cell RNA in both infected cell types are comparable (Figure 6—figure supplement 3).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: Only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected HepG2-NTCP cells and PHHs.
source_text: The levels of viral DNA in the media resulted from the ongoing infection during days 4–13 post-infection were low (equivalent to ∼1% of input viral DNA copies) despite significant amount of HBeAg secretion during this period. Similarly, only low levels of viral DNA were detected in the medium from HBV-infected PHHs
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by viral DNA quantification data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 4.

claim: Very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs inoculated with culture medium from infected HepG2-NTCP cells.
source_text: In line with the low HBV viral DNA level in the medium inoculum, very low number of intracellular HBV total RNA copies were detected in PHHs on day 13 post-infection (Figure 6—figure supplement 5)
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 5.

claim: Crab-eating monkey NTCP (mkNTCP) does not support pre-S1 binding or HDV infection.
source_text: Crab-eating monkey (Macaca fascicularis) NTCP (mkNTCP) shares 96% protein sequence identity with hNTCP but does not support pre-S1 binding or HDV infection (Figure 7A).
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A.

claim: Replacing aa 157–165 of mkNTCP with human counterpart rendered mkNTCP an efficient receptor for pre-S1 binding and HDV infection.
source_text: Replacing aa 157–165 of mkNTCP with human counterpart rendered mkNTCP an efficient receptor for pre-S1 binding and HDV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7A demonstrating gain of function.

claim: All NTCP variants expressed comparable levels of NTCP on cell surface.
source_text: All NTCP variants expressed comparable levels of NTCP.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 7B confirming equal expression levels.

claim: Replacing aa 157–165 of mkNTCP with human residues conferred its ability to support HBV infection.
source_text: HepG2 cells were transfected with plasmids encoding hNTCP, mkNTCP, or hNTCP variants bearing the indicated monkey residues, or mkNTCP variants with the indicated human residues. Transfected cells were maintained in PMM for 24 hr, and subsequently infected with HBV at 100 mge. HBeAg and HBV 3.5 kb RNA were assayed on 6 dpi.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7C demonstrating gain of function for HBV infection.

claim: Residues 157 to 165 of hNTCP are critical for pre-S1 binding and viral infections.
source_text: NTCP residues 157 to 165 were identified to be critical for pre-S1 binding and viral infections.
evidence_reasoning: This conclusion is based on mutagenesis data showing these residues are necessary and sufficient for receptor function.

claim: NTCP (Slc10a1) is the founding member of the SLC10 family of solute carrier proteins.
source_text: NTCP (Slc10a1) is the founding member of the SLC10 family of solute carrier proteins.
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about NTCP's classification.

claim: NTCP is a hepatic Na+ bile acid symporter responsible for cotransportation of sodium and bile acids across cellular membranes to maintain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids.
source_text: It is a hepatic Na+ bile acid symporter and is responsible for cotransportation of sodium and bile acids across cellular membranes to maintain the enterohepatic circulation of bile acids
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about NTCP's physiological function, supported by citations (Hagenbuch and Meier, 1994; Stieger, 2011).

claim: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane glycoprotein presumed to span the cellular membrane up to 10 times with small extracellular loops.
source_text: NTCP is a multiple transmembrane glycoprotein presumed to span the cellular membrane up to 10 times with small extracellular loops
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about NTCP structure, supported by citations (Mareninova et al., 2005; Hu et al., 2011).

claim: NTCP is mainly expressed in the liver.
source_text: It is mainly expressed in the liver (Stieger, 2011), consistent with the liver tropism of HBV and HDV.
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about NTCP tissue distribution, supported by citation.

claim: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes.
source_text: NTCP localizes to the sinusoidal (basolateral) plasma membrane of hepatocytes (Stieger et al., 1994)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about NTCP subcellular localization, supported by citation.

claim: HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate.
source_text: Whereas HBV first attaches to hepatocytes mainly through heparan sulfate (Schulze et al., 2007; Leistner et al., 2008)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge about initial HBV attachment, supported by citations.

claim: The interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific.
source_text: our data demonstrate that the interaction between NTCP and L protein of HBV is highly specific
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the specificity demonstrated by the WTb vs N9Kb peptide experiments and competition assays.

claim: NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes.
source_text: NTCP is crucial for productive viral entry of hepatocytes
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the combined knockdown and complementation experiments showing NTCP is necessary and sufficient for infection.

claim: NTCP expression rapidly decreased over time in cultured PTHs after isolation.
source_text: Consistent with previous reports on primary cultures of rat hepatocytes (Liang et al., 1993; Rippin et al., 2001), NTCP expression rapidly decreased over time in cultured PTHs after isolation.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data in Figure 2C and consistent with cited literature.

claim: Primary hepatocytes typically remain susceptible to HBV infections in vitro for only a few days after isolation from liver tissues.
source_text: This may at least partially explain the observations that primary hepatocytes typically remain susceptible to HBV infections in vitro for only a few days after isolation from liver tissues (Gripon et al., 1988; Seeger et al., 2007).
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from cited literature, and the connection to NTCP expression is inferred from the data.

claim: NTCP is functionally conserved in mammals.
source_text: NTCP is functionally conserved in mammalians
evidence_reasoning: This is general knowledge about NTCP conservation across species.

claim: Protein sequences of NTCP vary among species.
source_text: but protein sequences of NTCP vary among species
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by sequence comparison data and general knowledge.

claim: NTCP sequence variation likely contributes to the narrow species tropism of viral infection.
source_text: which is likely to contribute to the narrow species tropism of viral infection
evidence_reasoning: This is inferred from the mutagenesis data showing species-specific residues determine receptor function.

claim: Monkey NTCP shares 96% protein sequence identity with human NTCP but does not support HBV and HDV infection.
source_text: Strikingly, despite the high level of protein sequence homology between human and monkey NTCP, the later did not support HBV and HDV infection.
evidence_reasoning: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma.
source_text: NTCP expression is low and inversely correlated with the degree of dedifferentiation of cancer cells in human hepatocellular carcinoma (Kullak-Ublick et al., 1997; Zollner et al., 2005)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from cited literature about NTCP expression in cancer.

claim: NTCP expression is inversely correlated with the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis.
source_text: and the severity of HBV-related liver cirrhosis (Lee and Kim, 2007)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from cited literature about NTCP expression in cirrhosis.

claim: HepaRG is the only cell line known to date to be susceptible to HBV and HDV infections upon differentiation.
source_text: Human hepatoma cell line HepaRG is the only cell line known to date to be susceptible to HBV and HDV infections upon differentiation into a mixture of hepatocyte-like and biliary-like cells (Gripon et al., 2002).
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from cited literature about HepaRG cells.

claim: HepaRG differentiation requires maintaining undifferentiated cells for 2 weeks before induction, followed by induction with corticoids and DMSO for another 2–4 weeks.
source_text: HepaRG differentiation requires a lengthy cell culture procedure, including maintaining undifferentiated cells for 2 weeks before induction, followed by induction with corticoids and DMSO for another 2–4 weeks (Gripon et al., 2002).
evidence_reasoning: This is established protocol from cited literature for HepaRG differentiation.

claim: Efficient HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells in vitro normally requires high dose of virus inoculums.
source_text: Efficient HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells in vitro normally requires high dose of virus inoculums
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from cited literature (Gripon et al., 1988; Gripon et al., 2002; Boehm et al., 2005).

claim: Only limited progeny viruses are produced after HBV infection of PHHs or HepaRG cells.
source_text: and only limited progeny viruses are produced after infection (Gripon et al., 1988; Gripon et al., 2002; Boehm et al., 2005)
evidence_reasoning: This is established knowledge from cited literature about HBV infection in vitro.

claim: A Tupaia hepatocyte protein database was established by deep sequencing of the transcriptome.
source_text: The tandem mass spectra were searched against a Tupaia hepatocyte protein database, which we had established by deep sequencing of the transcriptome (Figure 2—figure supplements 1–4).
